questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -8+k \\ 3 & 5k\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2k$ is  $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -8+k \\ 3 & 5k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =2k[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}k-10 \\ -6+5k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4k \\ 2k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}k-10=-4k, \\ -6+5k=2k\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
k-10=-4k\,⟹\,k=2.
$$

Now, substituting $k=2$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6+5k & =2k \\ -6+5(2) & =2(2) \\ 4 & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=2.$

questions.worked_solution:
The conditional statement $P⇒Q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $¬P∨Q:$

So, in this case, we have the following equivalence:

$$
¬(A⇒B)≡¬(¬A∨B)
$$

Distributing the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law, we have

$$
¬(¬A∨B)≡¬(¬A)∧¬B.
$$

Canceling out double negation, we reach

$$
A∧¬B.
$$

So the given statement is equivalent to $A∧¬B.$

questions.problem:
A fair coin is flipped $5$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that the coin lands on heads at most $3$ times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the coin lands on heads.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ flips.

- The probability of landing heads is $p=\frac{1}{2}.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,\frac{1}{2}).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at most $3$ of the $5$ flips are heads. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{0}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{4} \\  & \,+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =(1+5+10+10)\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{5} \\  & =26\cdot \frac{1}{32} \\  & =0.813,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
